title: Open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket with high thrust and multi-thousand-second specific impulse

concept.text: An open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket would heat hydrogen using radiation from a fissioning uranium plasma, then expand the hot propellant through a nozzle to produce thrust. Specific impulse measures thrust per unit of propellant weight flow; higher values mean less exhaust mass is needed for a given thrust over time. The intended advance is to combine substantial thrust with specific impulse measured in thousands of seconds.

The gaseous fuel would occupy a region inside the engine cavity while hydrogen flows around it and absorbs its radiation. Unlike a solid-core nuclear thermal rocket, the concept would not require the fission fuel to remain a hot solid. Unlike a closed-cycle gas-core design, it would not enclose the uranium behind a solid transparent barrier. That open arrangement makes retaining the uranium while allowing heated hydrogen to escape a central engineering problem. The supplied historical evidence describes a feasibility concept and separate supporting investigations, not an operating integrated gas-core rocket.

significance.text: The potentially revolutionary capability is high exhaust velocity together with substantial thrust. Radiation from gaseous fission fuel offers a route to propellant temperatures that cannot be reached simply by making solid reactor fuel hotter. The March 1971 NASA report discussed estimated specific impulses from a minimum-interest value near 2000 seconds to perhaps 7000 seconds, while emphasizing that reliable performance predictions required further work. Realizing that capability with practical engine mass and manageable uranium consumption could substantially change the propulsion options for large interplanetary spacecraft.

The report illustrates the possible mission benefit with a modeled Mars round trip: a 5000-second gas-core engine, producing approximately 22 kN of thrust, reduced trip time from 500 days to 200 days relative to an 825-second solid-core engine. Both vehicles began at an initial mass of 770000 kg. This was an illustrative analysis based on unpublished NASA-Lewis work, not a demonstrated mission. It supports a conditional travel-time advantage at equal initial vehicle mass; it does not establish mass savings at the proposed 2500-second demonstration threshold, a particular one-way crew transit time, or a Mars trip under three months.

Synthesis: faster missions carrying large payloads, including missions beyond Mars, are plausible downstream possibilities if the engine can sustain its performance within a workable spacecraft mass budget. A successful short engine test would establish only part of that case. Mission-duration fuel retention, hydrogen storage, reactor integration, flight safety, and management of fuel-bearing radioactive exhaust would still determine practical usefulness. High specific impulse alone does not establish short travel times or an economically attractive transportation system.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated fission-powered engine that maintains enough gaseous uranium for the required criticality state while transferring substantial heat into flowing hydrogen and producing useful thrust. The 1971 report treated critical mass, fuel-region size, uranium loss, radiative heat transfer, and wall protection as linked feasibility questions. Success in an isolated criticality experiment or an electrically heated flow simulation would not establish that these requirements can be met together.

Fuel retention and heat transfer must work simultaneously. Hydrogen must absorb enough radiation to become an effective high-temperature propellant, while the flow must retain sufficient uranium and avoid excessive fuel consumption. The report considered hydrogen seeded with radiation-absorbing material as part of the wall-protection problem. Cavity walls and the nozzle retain material temperature limits even though the fuel itself is gaseous; moving beyond solid-fuel temperature limits does not eliminate the need to control heat reaching engine structures.

Synthesis and unresolved qualification: a convincing engine must establish how fuel-region stability and uranium loss behave under its intended operating conditions. The earlier research raises Earth-gravity distortion of the fuel region as a possible test complication, but the supplied review does not establish or quantify that effect. Its importance, and the extent to which a ground test would represent flight operation, therefore remain questions rather than demonstrated barriers of a known magnitude.

current_state.text: Robert G. Ragsdale's March 1971 NASA report, covering open-cycle gas-core work through 1970, describes basic-feasibility research supported by separate criticality, flow, and heat-transfer investigations. These included critical configurations and electrically heated flow simulations. Its estimate of potential specific impulse up to approximately 7000 seconds was explicitly provisional: further theoretical and experimental work was needed to determine engine performance reliably. The supplied evidence does not document an integrated fission-powered gas-core rocket demonstration.

Solid-core nuclear thermal propulsion has a different experimental history. Harold P. Gerrish Jr.'s May 9, 2022 NASA briefing reports that Rover/NERVA designed, built, and tested 20 reactors. Its dedicated program slide gives 1956–1973, while another slide uses 1955–1972, supporting an approximate description of work from the mid-1950s into the early 1970s. The fuel-development slide lists best possible capabilities of approximately 860 seconds of specific impulse for two hours and 20 starts, and approximately 875 seconds for one hour and three starts. These are stated fuel-performance capabilities; that slide alone does not establish measured integrated-engine performance at both operating points. The briefing also describes a solid-core development goal above 2700 K reactor exit temperature, corresponding to more than 900 seconds, rather than an achieved flight result.

A June 27, 2025 Breaking Defense article by Theresa Hitchens reports DARPA's cancellation of DRACO. It attributes deputy director Rob McHenry's weakening return-on-investment assessment partly to falling launch costs relative to the cost of developing nuclear thermal propulsion. This is a dated report about a nuclear thermal propulsion project; it does not establish the worldwide status of gas-core research. The article alone also does not independently establish DRACO's fuel architecture. A solid-core flight demonstration would remain distinct from the open-cycle gas-core capability defined here.

The evidence available here has important boundaries. The supplied review reports that portions of the 1971 PDF lacked extractable text and that equations and figure material were damaged in extraction; those portions were not inspected. Its accessible passages support the historical findings above, but cannot resolve every technical detail. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search establishing whether a gaseous fission core subsequently operated as a rocket through November 1, 2026. The record therefore supports a historical feasibility account, not a definitive present-day claim that no such demonstration has ever occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: operate an open-cycle gaseous uranium core that heats hydrogen predominantly through fission power and delivers measured specific impulse of at least 2500 seconds at thrust of at least 20 kN for at least five continuous minutes. These are proposed thresholds, not established standards or reported achievements. They would test an integrated capability substantially beyond the solid-core performance figures discussed in the supplied evidence, but would not by themselves validate the historical 5000-second mission comparison.
completion_criteria.label: Fission-powered operation sustains ≥2500-second specific impulse and ≥20-kN thrust for five minutes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: report the criticality state, fission-power contribution, any external power or neutron-source contribution, operating conditions, thrust history, and measurement uncertainties. Calculate specific impulse using total exhaust mass, including uranium and any other expelled material, rather than hydrogen alone. Report uranium loss relative to hydrogen flow, cumulative fuel consumption, and whether the fuel inventory and thermal conditions remain stable throughout the run. Near-critical operation would need enough information to distinguish fission-powered propulsion from a predominantly externally heated simulation.
completion_criteria.label: Report fission-power attribution and total-exhaust accounting with measurement uncertainties

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and operating-boundary requirements: repeat the integrated result with independently reviewable instrumentation, calibration, and mass-and-energy accounting. Demonstrate that the result can be reproduced across a declared operating envelope, including relevant startup, shutdown, and sustained-flow conditions. Report wall and nozzle temperatures, hardware condition after testing, and the conditions under which fuel retention deteriorates. Such finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, not universal stability at all scales, accelerations, or mission durations.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce integrated performance across declared operating envelope with reviewable accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical follow-through: establish an acceptable uranium-loss budget for a specified mission, justify how ground-test conditions represent intended flight operation, and evaluate engine mass, hydrogen requirements, exhaust management, and flight safety. A mission-performance claim would require a spacecraft and trajectory analysis using measured engine characteristics. These additional demonstrations would determine whether the initial breakthrough can become a useful propulsion system; the five-minute threshold alone would not establish operational readiness.
completion_criteria.label: Establish acceptable mission uranium-loss budget and evaluate propulsion-system practicality

related_concepts.text: Solid-core nuclear thermal propulsion and closed-cycle gas-core propulsion are the closest technical comparisons, although neither is a separate entry in the supplied roster. Solid-core engines heat propellant using solid reactor fuel and have a historical ground-test record. Closed-cycle gas-core concepts enclose gaseous uranium within a solid transparent barrier. Open-cycle gas-core propulsion instead depends on retaining fuel without that enclosure. The supplied evidence supports this containment distinction but does not quantify a temperature or performance penalty for the closed-cycle alternative.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-05, “Fission-fragment rocket with direct conversion of fragment momentum into thrust,” shares fission as its energy source but seeks thrust directly from fragment momentum. ROC-04 transfers fission energy into hydrogen and obtains thrust from the heated exhaust. Establishing either mechanism would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-02, “Beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit,” and ROC-03, “A directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed,” overlap with ROC-04 in using radiation within a propulsion system. Their defining energy source is an external beam; ROC-04 generates fission energy onboard and transfers radiation internally to propellant. ROC-01, “Sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed,” concerns atmospheric propulsion and the transition toward orbital flight, whereas ROC-04 concerns a gaseous-fission rocket engine. Their demonstration goals remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-06, “A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind,” and ROC-07, “An operational momentum-exchange tether that moves payloads between orbits,” pursue momentum transfer through the solar wind and tether dynamics, respectively. ROC-04 instead expels onboard heated propellant. They share the broader objective of changing spacecraft velocity but do not resolve its criticality, uranium-retention, or radiative-heating problems.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-08, “Industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth,” could complement ROC-04 through propellant supply if a compatible off-Earth hydrogen supply and loading system were developed. That infrastructure would address logistics rather than demonstrate the engine. Conversely, a successful gas-core engine would not establish industrial off-Earth propellant production.

unresolved_issues: Whether an integrated gaseous-fission rocket demonstration occurred after the historical report remains unestablished by the supplied evidence through November 1, 2026.
The magnitude and operational importance of Earth-gravity distortion of the fuel region, and the flight representativeness of ground testing, remain unresolved.
Achievable integrated specific impulse, thrust, engine mass, sustained operating duration, and uranium consumption remain undemonstrated in the supplied gas-core evidence.
The proposed initial demonstration does not specify an acceptable uranium-loss fraction; that boundary requires a stated mission and fuel budget.
The exact integrated-engine performance represented by the 2022 briefing's fuel-capability figures cannot be established from that slide alone.
Missing text and damaged equations and figures in the supplied 1971 extraction leave some technical details outside the reviewed evidence.

The supplied sources do not quantify the closed-cycle alternative's temperature or performance penalty, substantiate the chemical benchmark, or establish the earlier under-three-month Mars criterion. These details were omitted without treating them as disproven.
No separate modern roster-entry evidence was supplied; related-concept comparisons beyond the historical nuclear-propulsion distinctions are limited to synthesis from the supplied titles.

brief.title: A powerful rocket that needs much less propellant
possible: Large spacecraft could carry heavy payloads on faster journeys to Mars and beyond. The proposed rocket would combine a strong push with fast exhaust, using less propellant to deliver that push over time.

Splitting uranium atoms in a hot gas would release radiation that heats flowing hydrogen. The hydrogen would escape through a nozzle while the engine retains the uranium without a solid enclosure. Specific impulse measures thrust per propellant weight flow; higher values mean less expelled mass for the same push over time.
why: Gaseous uranium could heat hydrogen beyond what solid nuclear fuel can tolerate. Combining that hotter exhaust with substantial thrust would expand the propulsion options for large interplanetary spacecraft.

sources.showed: The Rover/NERVA programme built and tested reactors using solid fuel. This establishes a history of nuclear rocket testing with a different fuel arrangement.
sources.quote:
20 NTP different reactors designed 
built and tested during Rover/NERVA
sources.cited_for: Rockets heated by solid nuclear fuel provide an experimental comparison.
sources.not_established: Tests with solid fuel do not establish that a rocket can retain gaseous uranium while expelling hot hydrogen.

sources.who: Robert G. Ragsdale, NASA Lewis Research Center
sources.showed: Separate reactor experiments, flow simulations and heat-transfer studies explored feasibility. Air-flow experiments indicated potentially low uranium loss, but did not reproduce a working nuclear rocket.
sources.quote:
Flow experiments using air/air 
indicate that the uranium consumption might be less than 1 percent of the hydrogen propellant 
requirement.
sources.cited_for: The physical concept and the separate experiments supporting its feasibility.
sources.not_established: The studies did not demonstrate fuel retention, nuclear heating, useful thrust and protected engine walls working together.

sources.showed: Hitchens reported that DARPA cancelled its DRACO nuclear propulsion project after judging that its costs no longer matched the benefits.
sources.cited_for: Development cost and falling launch costs can change the practical case for nuclear propulsion.
sources.not_established: Cancelling a separate nuclear propulsion project does not establish the technical feasibility or research status of a gaseous-fuel rocket.

shown: Ragsdale’s NASA report describes experiments on sustaining a nuclear chain reaction, retaining fuel in flowing gas and transferring heat. Some flow simulations used electrical heating. These studies tested separate parts of the concept; they did not demonstrate an integrated nuclear rocket.
missing: An integrated engine must retain enough gaseous uranium to sustain nuclear heating while producing useful thrust.
Hydrogen must absorb enough radiation while the engine keeps its walls and nozzle within their temperature limits.
Repeated operation must establish fuel consumption, hardware endurance and performance suitable for a specified mission.

milestones.label: Sustained nuclear thrust with high propellant efficiency
milestones.explanation: An engine would have to sustain at least 2500 seconds of specific impulse while meeting the proposed thrust and run-duration thresholds, mainly using nuclear heat. This would establish integrated performance.

milestones.label: Measured nuclear power and complete exhaust accounting
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to distinguish nuclear heat from external power and count all expelled material, including uranium, with stated uncertainties. This would establish credible performance and fuel-loss figures.

milestones.label: Repeatable performance across stated operating conditions
milestones.explanation: Repeated tests would have to reproduce performance across stated startup, shutdown and sustained-flow conditions, with reviewable measurements and hardware checks. This would establish where the engine works and fuel retention fails.

milestones.label: A workable propulsion system for a specified mission
milestones.explanation: A mission assessment would have to establish acceptable uranium loss, representative testing, engine mass, hydrogen needs, exhaust management and flight safety using measured performance. This would determine practical usefulness.

uncertain: How strongly would Earth’s gravity distort the uranium region, and how well would ground tests represent operation in flight?
How much uranium loss could a specified mission tolerate?
Can high propellant efficiency and substantial thrust persist for mission-length operation within a workable engine mass?
